Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise reflects fear, vigilance, avoidance of proximity/anger cues, and beliefs that others may harm her. In that context, endorsing risky or self-endangering behavior is hard to reconcile clinically, especially with no Maladaptive Strategies items or other disinhibition/externalising content to support it.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, a global appraisal that 'you can never know who will harm you' is possible but sits somewhat awkwardly beside highly specific interpersonal triggers (physical proximity, others' anger) and trauma-linked memory content. It implies diffuse unpredictability of all potential perpetrators rather than the more coherent expected pattern of threat from close others or angry interpersonal situations.

vignette: At 77, Amara, a proud African‑American woman who has spent decades campaigning in the heart of her community, recalls the night that forever altered the way she walks through a room. When her then‑partner, a former business executive, let his anger flare into physical violence, the sheer proximity of his clenched fists and the sudden splatter of blood left an indelible imprint. Even now, a glance at a person’s face when they raise their voice—whether it is a colleague at a committee meeting or a campaign staffer arguing over strategy—triggers the same raw instinct that had driven her to flee the house that night. That instinct sends a surge of threat into her: she feels unsafe even after the lights come on, her heart racing in the dark of her bedroom, and she begins to look over her shoulder whenever she walks home from a fundraiser. The trigger also pulls at the fragments of memory that she has carried for years—images of her partner’s hands on her shoulders, the taste of metal on her tongue, and a sense that the story is unfinished. These memories, though incomplete, amplify the belief that the violence has permanently changed her, that her emotions are dulled, and that people cannot be trusted. The weight of those negative appraisals does not merely sit in her mind; it informs every new threat she perceives. When a fellow senator bursts into anger over a budget proposal, Amara’s conviction that she has been forever damaged spikes, and she finds herself on edge, convinced that the same pattern might repeat. Her guilt over the event’s incomplete recollection also deepens, making the memory feel more elusive and more dangerous. As a result, she actively avoids any situation that might spark those old triggers: she declines speaking roles where passionate debate is expected, she keeps her phone out of reach during late nights, and she avoids crowds where people might inadvertently express frustration. These avoidance behaviors reinforce her sense that the world is hostile and that her own body is no longer safe. When Amara’s mind forces the fragmented memories to surface, they do not merely recollect the past; they re‑ignite the very threats that haunt her nights. A sudden startle at a flickering streetlamp reminds her of the moment she felt the weight of her partner’s hand. The guilt that floods her when she tries to piece the story together makes her feel as if she is perpetually falling short of a complete self. And the very sight of blood—whether in a hospital chart at a political health briefing or in the corner of a photograph—pushes her back into a state of heightened vigilance, as though her body were still braced for another assault. These memories therefore serve as triggers in their own right, looping back to the original sensations that began her cycle. The threat that now gnaws at her at dusk shapes her memories, her appraisals, and her reactions to the world. Late‑night, after a speech at a city hall, she hears a distant thud and immediately thinks of the hallway she fled from years ago. The memory surfaces abruptly, her mind filling in gaps with images of bruises and the echo of slammed doors. The persistent sense of danger tells her that people cannot be trusted, even a colleague she respects, because their anger might conceal violence. In the same breath, a sharp visual cue—a glint of red on a colleague’s sleeve—acts as a trigger, reminding her that the threat is real and present. Thus, the cycle tightens: the threat begets memory, memory feeds negative appraisal, and appraisal reinforces threat, each reinforcing the other. Now, amid the bustle of her campaign office, Amara has begun to seek help because the perpetual night vigilance has begun to erode her effectiveness as a public servant. She fears that if she cannot quiet the alarm in her own mind, she will lose the sharpness required to draft legislation and the compassion needed to connect with constituents. Yet she also holds a fragile hope that, with the right support, she can reclaim the sense of safety that has eluded her for decades, allowing her to breathe freely on the campaign trail and, ultimately, to serve her community without the constant shadow of past violence.
